title: Is being an "art director" for AI game devs a viable service idea for me as an artist?
author: Nima-tries-to-draw
selftext:
Figured I'd ask here. I browsing through AI games and I noticed a common pain point (in the visibly AI ones) is 

1. the lack of a unified art direction between assets. They don't look made by the same person.

2. the art direction is the default style of chatgpt 

Animation studios often use [style guides](https://maddogmovies.com/2025/01/17/animation-style-guides/) to get all the artists drawing in the same style. Does that sound helpful in this case?

It's a difficult market rn. Let me know if you think an artist specialising in fixing, redoing AI game art and giving it an art direction could be a viable job in this changing industry.

comments.author: Super_Range45
comments.body: When making a game, you should generally create gameplay first and only focus on graphics after the gameplay is engaging and complete.

replies.author: Nima-tries-to-draw
replies.body: Sure, but I can't offer feedback on that more than the average person. I can on art though.

comments.author: Kaelzoroden
comments.body:
Honestly I think that's where the art departments for game studios are headed. AI gives anyone the ability to make something that looks relatively polished, but the skills of an artist in regards to creative vision, style choices, composition and flow, etc, are what is lacking in so much slop-looking AI stuff.

My prediction is that the art team of a half-decade from now is going to consist of a few such art directors guiding AIs to produce AAA-levels of polish on Indie-levels of weird and original ideas, done on indie-levels of budget.

comments.author: lithander
comments.body: Yeah I think it is. Maybe also consulting sessions for hobby devs.

replies.author: Nima-tries-to-draw
replies.body: Consulting sessions sound like a good idea.

comments.author: captainlispers
comments.body: Id actually pay for this. The only issue that I find with stuff like this is Ai can do a whole bunch and make changed galore. But not having ai art and being able to actually have more human involvement is always worth it

comments.author: vug_undertherug
comments.body: Probably if you find the right person. I’ve been working for several months on a project. My visuals are behind partly because of the limitations of AI, but I’m also learning how to achieve styling consistency. It’s easy to get something a lot of people would say “good enough”, or for a prototype, but it’s substantially harder to do much better than that. I have a pretty sophisticated workflow/system I’ve put together just for 2D visuals, and the output generally feels 90% there and that last 10% is the big hurdle. But it’s worth separating out here, a lot of people are doing this as a hobby or side project, probably with very limited budget. I would love artist support but the reality is I cant actually afford it.

replies.author: Nima-tries-to-draw
replies.body: Do you mind sharing some of your work?

comments.author: TirOrin13
comments.body:
IMO the Art and UI polish are the hardest part. Outside of just having a good gameplay loop and a better idea which is AI-agnostic.

I've been working on my game for quite a while now, and, as an engineer I can say the coding nearly solved (especially if you already know what you're looking at). The art direction and vibe of games is probably gonna end up being the most difficult and important thing in the coming years.

comments.author: Jolly-Rip5973
comments.body:
more than likely you would be one the generating the assets that though. 

The dev making the game isn't take the time to generate 6000 assets for you to approve or disapprove each one. 

It far more efficient and workable for you to use Ai to make them yourself.

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body: yes, that is one of the best paths for good artists to work with AI. it takes a massive amount of time and effort getting the AI to stick to an art style and polish the art with a lot of engineer-minded folks or new developers not really being able to do it as it takes a lot of taste and knowledge. An artist who wants to use AI and direct the entire art pipeline is hugely desirable

comments.author: PersonOfInterest007
comments.body:
It certainly should be a valuable service. I think the challenge will be finding people to pay for it, because I think may devs who use AI for art are doing so specifically because they can't afford an artist.  

Note that you might also try to work with devs who use asset packs rather than AI, since they have similar challenges -- how to make assets from different packs appear cohesive.  You've got the same affordability issue, but it is an additional source of clients.

I recommend posting in r/gameDevClassifieds and r/INAT.

replies.author: Nima-tries-to-draw
replies.body: Didn't think about asset pack users. I wonder what name I could give to a service like that.

replies.author: PersonOfInterest007
replies.body:
If the community doesn’t have a better name, I’d go with something like “Game art consultant,” and say you do things like help choose an overall art style, making separate assets cohesive, modifying or improving existing art, or perhaps even finding other artists, or whatever else you think you could do.

I would strongly recommend against even mentioning AI in any way. There are very strong and vocal contingents among players, devs, and artists that are anti-AI, and you’d probably get excommunicated from the art community for saying you’re actually going to help devs use AI for art.  I’m not saying you can’t end up helping people whose AI if they privately ask you, but do yourself a big favor and don’t publicize it.

replies.author: Nima-tries-to-draw
replies.body:
>you’d probably get excommunicated from the art community for saying you’re actually going to help devs use AI for art.

My idea originally is add human touch to it rather than use more AI. But yeah I understand it's a controversial topic.

Thanks for the ideas!

comments.author: Glittering-Kick-7251
comments.body: This would definitely help a lot of people and is a viable market. In fact I think that's how most game artists will be working in the future. I think for people to pay, you'll need to be able to get actual production ready output based on the style guide. I would definitely spend money for an easier way to generate consistent set of assets.

replies.author: Nima-tries-to-draw
replies.body: It will take some exploration to figure out how to develop a style guide that an AI and an AI-assisted developer could both understand but it's good that there's interest.

comments.author: TGG_brian
comments.body: Would you wanna message me with some rates and examples? Would definitely be interested for a project I'm working on!

comments.author: phira
comments.body:
I suspect yes. To be honest it's probably even more valuable than it appears - the AI tools let the devs create playgrounds where an Art Director could help explore options, or alternatively the Art Director could do the same. While building Solar Trader I had a variety of art things to figure out, and I got Astra to make little labs for them:

[https://solar-trader-haven.phir.chatgpt.site/engine-lab](https://solar-trader-haven.phir.chatgpt.site/engine-lab)

[https://solar-trader-haven.phir.chatgpt.site/planet-lab](https://solar-trader-haven.phir.chatgpt.site/planet-lab) (might take a bit to load, there's shaders)

where I could play and then integrate back into the game itself. The labs don't need to be part of the same codebase, but really handy to be able to have it sitting there in context, interactable etc. Then you get to bring the Taste/Judgement element to the table.

All that is on top of concepts, style guides etc. Might make sense to partner with a sound/music person too, and offer a set of different ways of working together to match the different kinds of demand - early concept work, pre-testing review, later stage review and polish for people looking to head into Early Access or build market visibility.   
  
Using a lot of AI in your own workflow would avoid having some of those tasks take so long that devs get priced out - there's still room for solid human work at a higher price point for those who want or need it of course. The key thing is not to delegate everything to the AI though, people are paying for your taste and judgement not just a better prompted ChatGPT.

comments.author: KnownPride
comments.body:
Yes, because your job is artstyle direction.  
The only diff if before under you is 15 people now it's 5 people with ai.

comments.author: 12redandblack12
comments.body: i think that's a good service to offer for ai devs if you have a portfolio and can pin down exactly what you can offer. asking chatgpt/ai is useless for any feedback because you can show it a stick figure and it will just glaze you. human consultation and feedback is important.

comments.author: Dekker3D
comments.body:
Uh, I think this might be viable. My honest take is that you might want to learn how to work with AI and kinda do it like this:  
\- Rest of team comes to you with requirements for art and their best attempt at generating the asset, including prompts, workflow, etc.  
\- You check it out to find out what's inconsistent with the rest of the art, what parts just scream "I was spat out by AI", and what parts need improvements in general; all stuff that's pretty easy to fix... but also: when something just doesn't work, aesthetically, for reasons that the average person might not fully grasp. Colour theory, that sort of thing.  
\- Depending on the issues, you either hand it back to them with your observations, to rethink the art entirely, or you can fix it or tell them how to fix it.

I've been drawing for ages, doing 3D art for just about as long, and I've taught a few people in both. Never got very successful with it (I've got some crippling ADD + some milder autistic traits), but those skills combine really well with AI skills to create cool stuff. It already feels a bit like being an "art director". I think there'd be some overlap.

Also, a thing that's easily missed: if you give AI a simple prompt, it will fill in the blanks with generic stuff. Feeding it a handmade sketch or just redoing part of it by splashing some blobs of colour onto key parts, can make a huge difference in making it feel more natural. Obviously training a LoRA for your project's art style can also help. I'm using all of those techniques for my own current project.

comments.author: Difficult_Ad_2314
comments.body: As someone that is doing game development using AI, I would argue that I would rather have a proper 3d artist doing the 3d modelling and the artwork rather than using AI, since I feel like, from my experience, AI-generated models still lacking, and even if the AI has reached to the point of professional quality, i believe human-made models would be more preferable as it is easier to work with actual artist than the AI prompts. Though I am using AI for my models because it is cheaper, I would like to hire proper 3D artists for my bigger games in the future.

comments.author: thygrrr
comments.body: At the place I work our art director is former Disney and has embraced AI and overpaints etc. basically fully. It definitely is a field you can work in, and art direction is certainly not trivial.

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body: Starving art director id going to be the new starving artist.
